title: Market day
goal: I can read and write money in dollars and cents. I can pay exactly, find every way, give change and work backwards.

learn.intro: Money is written in dollars and cents. $1 is 100¢, so $3.45 is 345¢. To pay exactly with the fewest pieces, take the greatest note or coin that fits, again and again.

example.problem: A cake costs $4.35. Pay the exact amount with as few notes and coins as you can.
steps: Dollars first: $4 is $2 + $2. That is 2 notes.
Now the cents: 35¢. The greatest coin that fits is 20¢. 15¢ is left.
The greatest coin that fits 15¢ is 10¢. Then 5¢ is left: one 5¢ coin.

howto.title: How to pay exactly
steps: Split the cost into dollars and cents.
Take the greatest note or coin that fits.
Add to check. Count the pieces.

try.text: Pay exactly $6.85 with as few notes and coins as you can. How many pieces? {b}

items.text: Change dollars and cents.
items.explanation: $1 is 100¢. (a) 3 dollars is 300¢, and 300 + 45 = 345. (b) 275¢ is 2 dollars and 75 cents: $2.75. (c) 6 dollars and 5 cents is $6.05, not $6.50. (d) 100¢ + 30¢ = 130¢.

items.text: Count the money. How much is there altogether?
Pay the exact amount with as few notes and coins as you can. Write them on the lines. Then count the pieces.
items.explanation: Marker pen: $2 + 50¢ + 20¢ + 10¢ + 5¢ is 5 pieces. Kite: $5 + $2 + 20¢ + 20¢ is 4 pieces. Backpack: $10 + $10 + $2 + $1 + 50¢ + 10¢ + 5¢ is 7 pieces (there is no $20 note).

items.text: Find EVERY way to pay exactly $7 using $1 coins, $2 notes and $5 notes. Begin with as many $5 notes as you can. Write each way in a row. Some rows may stay empty.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The way with exactly 4 pieces has {b} $2 notes and {b} $1 coin.

items.explanation: Ways ($5, $2, $1): 1, 1, 0 / 1, 0, 2 / 0, 3, 1 / 0, 2, 3 / 0, 1, 5 / 0, 0, 7. That is 6 ways. Their pieces are 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 and 7. Only 0, 3, 1 has 4 pieces: three $2 notes and one $1 coin.

items.text: Find the change.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A ruler costs 70¢. Kumar pays with a $1 coin. Change: {b} ¢

parts.label: b
parts.text: A book costs $4.30. Mei pays with a $10 note. Change: $ {b}

parts.label: c
parts.text: A bag costs $37. Ali pays with a $50 note. Change: $ {b}

parts.label: d
parts.text: The fewest notes and coins for the $13 change: {b} pieces

items.explanation: Change is what you pay minus the cost. (a) 100¢ - 70¢ = 30¢. (b) $10 - $4.30 = $5.70. Count on: $4.30 to $5 is 70¢, then $5 more makes $10. (c) $50 - $37 = $13. (d) $13 is $10 + $2 + $1: 3 pieces.

Shop deals.
items.explanation: (a) 12 pencils is 3 groups of 4, so 3 × $1 = $3. (b) 20 stickers is 4 groups of 5, so 4 × $2 = $8. (c) $6 is 3 groups of $2, so 3 × 5 = 15 stickers.

items.text: Ali buys 2 toys for exactly $12.50. Which 2 toys? {b} and {b}
items.explanation: $4.50 + $8.00 = $12.50. Check the others: Car + Ball = $10.75, Car + Kite = $8.25, Ball + Top = $14.25, Ball + Kite = $10.00, Top + Kite = $11.75. Only Car and Top.

items.text: Mei pays exactly 95¢ with 4 coins. Use 5¢, 10¢, 20¢ or 50¢ coins. Write the coins. {b}¢ + {b}¢ + {b}¢ + {b}¢
items.explanation: Start with 50¢. 45¢ is left for 3 coins. 20¢ + 20¢ = 40¢, and 5¢ makes 45¢. Check: 50 + 20 + 20 + 5 = 95. No other 4 coins make 95¢.

items.text: Pay 35¢ with 5¢, 10¢ and 20¢ coins. List EVERY way in the table.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The 5-coin way: {b} coins of 10¢ and {b} of 5¢.

items.hint: Try 1 coin of 20¢ first. Then none. Fill the rest with 10¢ and 5¢.

items.text: Lollipops cost 20¢ each. Cookies cost 50¢ each. Siti buys 7 things and spends exactly $2.60. How many lollipops and how many cookies?
items.explanation: 7 lollipops cost $1.40. Each swap of a lollipop for a cookie adds 30¢: $1.70, $2.00, $2.30, $2.60. That is 4 swaps. So 3 lollipops and 4 cookies. Check: 60¢ + $2.00 = $2.60 and 3 + 4 = 7.
items.hint: Start with 7 lollipops. Swap one for a cookie each time.

items.text: A book costs $4 more than a puzzle. Together they cost $13.
items.explanation: Take away the extra $4: $13 - $4 = $9. Two equal bars share $9, so each is $4.50. The puzzle costs $4.50 and the book costs $4.50 + $4 = $8.50. Check: 4.50 + 8.50 = 13.00.
items.hint: Take away the extra $4. Share what is left equally.

items.text: Beyond: a shop sign says PAY HALF. You pay half of the amount on the tag.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A ball has a tag of $9.60. You pay $ {b}

parts.label: b
parts.text: A hat has a tag of $14.50. You pay $ {b}

parts.label: c
parts.text: A kite costs $5.80 with PAY HALF. The tag says $ {b}

items.explanation: (a) Half of $9.60 is $4.80. (b) Half of $14 is $7 and half of 50¢ is 25¢: $7.25. (c) The tag is double: $5.80 + $5.80 = $11.60.
items.hint: Half of dollars first. Then half of cents. Go back with double.

items.text: Mei has 5 coins. Each coin is 20¢ or 50¢.

parts.label: a
parts.text: How many different amounts could she have? {b}

parts.label: b
parts.text: With exactly 3 coins of 50¢, she has $ {b}

items.explanation: 5 coins of 20¢ is $1.00. Each swap of a 20¢ for a 50¢ adds 30¢: $1.00, $1.30, $1.60, $1.90, $2.20, $2.50. That is 6 amounts. (b) 3 coins of 50¢ and 2 of 20¢: $1.50 + $0.40 = $1.90. (c) $1.40 is not in the list: no.
items.hint: Start with 5 coins of 20¢. Swap one for 50¢ each time.

items.text: Make your own coin riddle. Choose 3 coins from 5¢, 10¢, 20¢ and 50¢ (a coin can be used twice). Write how much they are worth, so that only ONE set of 3 coins fits. Many answers are right.

answer.text: Open. Example: 3 coins are worth 80¢. Only 50¢, 20¢ and 10¢ fit.

items.explanation: Example: 3 coins worth 80¢. The only set is 50¢ + 20¢ + 10¢. Any other 3 coins make a different total. A riddle is good if no other set fits.
items.hint: Try all the sets of 3 coins. Does another set make the same total?

items.text: Shop A sells 3 pens for $2. Shop B sells 4 pens for $3. Ben wants 12 pens.
items.explanation: (a) 12 pens is 4 groups of 3, so 4 × $2 = $8. (b) 12 pens is 3 groups of 4, so 3 × $3 = $9. (c) $8 is less than $9, so shop A is cheaper by $1.
items.hint: 12 pens is how many groups of 3? Of 4?
